title: Bass solo support, Elvin Jones's advice, and the Paris New Morning solo
summary: McBee wants sustained chords behind his solo, recalls Elvin Jones telling him to play that, and tells how the Leaders walked off in Paris leaving him to improvise on a tune he disliked.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: It reminds me, I recently was talking to a younger bass player and we were talking about bass solos and he expressed that he would get quite aggravated when it was time for the bass solo and everybody else just stopped. You know like okay, a cappella, it’s all on you and there’s no accompaniment and no support. And I wonder when you have your choice what do you like to have happen behind your bass solo?

Behind my bass solo — well first of all, if in tempo, the piano must sustain chords to support me. Don’t rhythmatize anything. Don’t play rhythmically you know. Just sustain, so I can have a carpet, I can hear where the changes are going. But other than that, it’s important to be able to express regardless of the situation. Like Elvin Jones used to tell me, he says, “McBee, if you don’t hear anything, if you don’t have anything to play, if you don’t feel nothing,” he says, “play that.”

He says, “If you’re soloing and you don’t feel like playing something, if you don’t feel comfortable with what you’re playing, play that.” Which means that given those special moments of practice, of study, that will come in, that vibe, that feeling of intent to be excellent will manifest itself somehow, even in the spirit of, you know — I tell my students, important is to after you play something if you don’t hear that, stop and look where you’re going because when you do that, stop. The spirit of it all of who you are will manifest and point the way for you. Right? In terms of how it feels. So but I’m reminded in Paris there’s a club called the New Morning Jazz Club. Maybe 150, 200 people sat in the place. I was with the leaders at the time and we were going to, after the concert, celebrate Kirk Lightsey’s birthday, he’s on piano. And so we’re performing a tune by Arthur Blythe that I couldn’t find anything ever to do with that tune because it was well with respected to Arthur, I did not like the tune. It was like C-C-C-C-Dflat-D-E- E-E-B-B-E-E-C forever. Right. Great melody but harmonically a little under. So I never soloed on it. So, and I guess the guys in the band knew that. So here we are, we’ve concluded all the solos and usually Don Moye would take a drum solo, right? And we’d walk away and let him do his thing. So at the conclusion of the piano solo I look up and Don Moye, the drummer, and all the guys are walking off the stage to leave me there you

know. And I said what the hell do I do? Here’s something I don’t like, I’m uncomfortable, and the people are like expecting the adventure of Cecil McBee. And what I did, I closed my eyes, literally, I just closed my eyes and went into my living room to where I usually would practice, and I played that. I put the tempo down and just played an open solo as though I would practice, and I ventured into this area and that area, and then I would balk a little bit, which would lead me into this you know, I really improvised. And it turned out rather well. So that was a trying moment for me in the eyes of the world in terms of who I really was, to make something happen out of nothing so to speak.
